text:
[quiet, close to the microphone, calm and unhurried, a man talking across a kitchen table late at night] — your light was on. I hope that's all right. I won't stay long.

[precise, patient, slightly pleased with his own clarity] I want to explain how I keep things. Then it'll make sense.

I'd had some of those windows open since March. February, some of them. Three of them were the same note... I closed two.

Everything goes side by side now. Nothing on top of anything. Mail went to two. The browser went to three. I went back to make sure. They were still there. There's a bar along the bottom, so you always know where everything is.

I made a rule. Chatter opens on two. [a small pause] I did read both messages.

I gave Mark his drill back. Four years. It's a better drill than mine, actually. He said I didn't need to.

Four is the house. Five is the street. Nobody else wanted to take the minutes.

[cooler, very even] Your hedge is six foot two. The limit is six feet. We've talked about it... twice. I've photographed it every morning since. A hundred and sixty mornings.

I sent the minutes round again. You're the only one who replied.

[colder, quieter, never louder] There was a photograph attached. It took me a minute to recognise the study. [pause] From this side.

[exhales] Can I sit? ...I'll sit.

[a long silence, then flat and soft] Leave it on.

A.note: Restrained. He explains how he keeps things, closes two of the three who signed, says where Sixteen and Mark are, and stops at “They're both on six.” The detective suspends the interview.

B.note: As A, then “Everything else had a place. He was the last thing.” and nothing more.

C.note: The full account: the night he went over, the plastic already down, and “He's on six now. With the others.”

D.note: Draft 5, audio only. One long take (d2 of ten), the detective's two questions put into the silences. The second “I closed two, and nothing happened.” is the first one's reading from the same take.

E1.note: Draft 10, audio only. One long take (e12 of twelve), the detective's two lines put into silences. The second “I closed two, and nothing happened.” is the first one's reading from the same take. Ends on “Do you use a Mac?”

E2.note: E1 cut after “It was her idea.”: the same take, then the detective suspends the interview.

H.note: Draft 13, audio only. One long take (h3 of eight), the detective's two questions put into silences opened for them. Ends on “You look like a man with a great many windows open.”

J2.note: Draft 15, the 2:00 cut. Take j1 of six, the most like tape H in pace; the silences between sentences trimmed to what a person leaves.

J1.note: Draft 15, the 1:30 cut: the 2:00 cut without the Alan line.

K.note: Draft 16: he says little, the screen shows the rest. It opens cold on his voice and ends on his last line: no detective at either end and no recorder tones, so it isn't clear it's an interview until the detective's two questions. Take k7 of eight (word-perfect, the most even in level, close to H's pace), with "From the start? All right." from s3 of six takes of the same opening in the same voice and direction. Silences opened after the lines the picture contradicts, so the picture can run past the words.

A.note: Restrained but unmistakable. No. 14 makes a faint “hm” after the odd phrase. He closed two of the three who signed the note, Mark “has a place”, and the sheets are down. Ends on “Leave it on.”

textD:
[a man in a police interview room, close to the table microphone, calm, unhurried, plain and procedural, speaking in complete sentences, quietly pleased with how well it all works] From the start? All right. It started with the windows. On my computer, I mean.

I had about forty of them open, and some had been open for a year. Three of them turned out to be the same note. I closed two, and nothing happened. I didn't even notice they were gone.

Then I installed a small program. It's called Spaceman.

The windows tiled themselves. They sat side by side, with nothing on top of anything and nothing behind anything, and I could see all of it at once. I tasted the sweet flesh of efficiency.

It gives you numbered workspaces. I put Messages on workspace two and the browser on three. You press a number, and a bar comes up along the bottom to show you where you are. People think that when a window isn't in front of them, it's gone. It isn't gone. It's on two. You press two, and there it is, exactly where you left it.

Then I made a rule, so that Messages always opens on two without asking me. A rule decides once, and then you never have to decide again. I liked that more than I expected to.

After that I couldn't stop noticing things that weren't where they belonged. I'd had my neighbour Mark's drill for four years. It's a better drill than mine, actually, but it had a place, and the place was his garage. So I walked it back.

Then I put cameras in the house and gave them workspace four: one window for each room. All but the cellar. That wasn't ready yet.

Workspace five was the street. I put up a camera for each house, in the order of the house numbers, so everyone on the street was on five. Two of those houses are empty now. I've left their windows where they were, so the order still holds.

[cooler, very even, never louder] Alan Pike, at number fourteen, had a hedge two inches over the HOA limit. I started keeping the HOA's minutes so that it would be written down properly, and I photographed it every morning for a hundred and sixty mornings. I can find any morning you like.

I left workspace six empty. It's good to have somewhere to put things.

[colder, quieter, level, never louder] Then three of the neighbours signed a note asking me to take the cameras down: Mark, Joan from number sixteen, and Alan. It was the same note, with three names on it. I closed two, and nothing happened. Nobody noticed either of them was gone for a week.

I moved Joan from five to six in March. I moved Mark in June, the afternoon I walked his drill back.

[level, reasonable, procedural] Alan was the last thing that didn't have a place. He came over late on Friday to talk about the hedge. He said he'd cut it at the weekend, and I believed him, actually. But I'd already put the plastic down, and I don't decide things twice.

You keep saying he's gone. He isn't gone.

[patiently, as if explaining something obvious] He's on six.

[level, cold, quietly pleased] One window. It's the camera in the cellar. All three of them are in it, side by side. Nothing on top of anything. Nothing behind anything.

[a beat; then sincerely, helpfully] Do you use a Mac?

textE:
[a man in a police interview room, close to the table microphone, warm, ordinary and likeable, a little self-deprecating, giving a sincere testimonial for a small app he loves, fond of his wife, speaking in complete sentences] From the start? Okay. It started with my computer. It was Claire's idea, actually. My wife. She said my desktop looked like a junk drawer, and she wasn't wrong.

I had about forty windows open, and three of them were the same note. I closed two, and nothing happened. I didn't even notice they were gone.

[genuinely happy, warm] So I installed a little app called Spaceman, and honestly, it's lovely. Every window tiled itself. Side by side. Nothing on top of anything, nothing behind anything. I sat there for an hour just opening things.

You get numbered workspaces. Messages went on two, Mail on three. Press a number, and a little bar comes up to show you where you are. If something's on the wrong one, you move it. And a window that isn't in front of you isn't gone. It's on two.

Then I made a rule, so Messages always opens on two. You decide once, and then it just happens. Claire said she wished I'd always been like that.

I did the same with my week. Sundays at seven, I answer messages. Claire's sister writes every Sunday, and she always gets an answer.

[a little plainer, even] I'd had Mark's drill from next door for four years. It belonged in his garage, so I walked it back.

Then I put cameras in the house. One window for each room, on workspace four. Not the cellar. That wasn't ready. Claire asked me which number she was. I think she was joking.

[flatter and more exact, never louder] Five is the street. A camera for every house, in number order. Mark's garage. Joan's cat, on the step at sixteen. Alan's hedge at fourteen, two inches over the limit. I photographed it at seven every morning. A hundred and sixty mornings.

The first night I had everyone on five, I didn't go to bed. I kept going through the workspaces until it got light.
